I want to start on /investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding. I am particularly interested in this direction. Can you explain it in more depth to start?
I’ll read the earlier discussion and the boundary-winding notes, then explain the idea, what it would need to prove, and where the main obstacle lies.

The central idea is to enclose a possible collision and study how the value-and-slope vector turns along the enclosure’s boundary. The useful feature is that every heat-flow collision contributes winding with the same sign, so different collisions cannot cancel each other’s contributions. I’m checking the precise conditions and the earlier comparison to distinguish what is already established from the new arithmetic work.

The earlier winding calculation worked, but on its test box direct certification was just as effective and slightly cheaper. The opportunity here is to find a boundary where the arithmetic is easier to control than it is inside. I’m also using the visualization skill to illustrate how walking around a region turns the value-and-slope vector around the origin.

One useful advantage is that the boundary calculation only needs to rule out one complete clockwise turn; it need not determine every angle precisely. The hard part remains proving that bound from the genuine arithmetic. A natural first question is whether we can surround an unresolved small-jet region with a boundary whose full image can be certified to have winding zero.

I read the earlier conversation and the [boundary-winding opening note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/notes/01_INITIAL_RESEARCH_NOTE_20261019.md). **The attraction of this direction is that it can exclude every collision inside a region using information only along its boundary.** This could be useful when the interior contains severe arithmetic cancellation, but a surrounding boundary is easier to control.

The decisive feature is that **every heat-flow collision contributes winding with the same sign**. Consequently, different collisions cannot hide by cancelling one another’s contributions.

Let me develop the picture and then identify the research opportunity.

There are two different planes involved. The first is the **time–position plane**, with coordinates \((t,x)\). A hypothetical collision is a point in this plane satisfying
\[
H(t,x)=H_x(t,x)=0.
\]

The second is the **value–slope plane**, whose coordinates are
\[
J(t,x)=\bigl(H(t,x),H_x(t,x)\bigr).
\]
A collision occurs precisely when this vector reaches the origin.

Here I am using the physical jet. The phase-scaled jet from our earlier discussion has related zero locations, but its effect on winding and orientation must be accounted for before transferring conclusions.

Now draw a closed boundary around a region \(D\) in the time–position plane. As we walk around that boundary, the corresponding vector \(J\) traces a closed curve in the value–slope plane. Provided it never reaches the origin, we can count its net turns around the origin:

- One counterclockwise turn gives winding \(+1\).
- One clockwise turn gives winding \(-1\).
- No net turn gives winding \(0\).

The boundary image can bend, retrace parts of itself, or cross itself. Winding records its **total signed turning around the origin**, rather than its geometric complexity.

A simple example makes the connection visible:
\[
H(t,x)=x^2-2t,
\qquad
J(t,x)=(x^2-2t,\,2x).
\]
This satisfies the same backward heat equation as the theta field,
\[
H_t=-H_{xx}.
\]
It has a double zero at \((0,0)\). Before that time there are no real roots; afterwards there are two.

Walking counterclockwise around a rectangle containing this event makes the jet wind once clockwise. The illustration lets you follow the walk and compare a region containing the event with one excluding it. This is an exact polynomial model, not a theta computation.

visualize{"path":"/Users/ebbaker/.codex/visualizations/2026/10/20/01a15728-862d-78e3-8f01-d3cf1e059d4e/boundary-winding.html"}

The reason the clockwise contribution persists for general double collisions is particularly clean. At a collision with \(H_{xx}\ne0\), the derivative of the jet map is
\[
D_{(t,x)}J
=
\begin{pmatrix}
-H_{xx}&0\\
-H_{xxx}&H_{xx}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det D_{(t,x)}J=-H_{xx}^{\,2}<0.
\]
Thus the map reverses orientation near the event: a small counterclockwise source loop becomes a clockwise target loop.

The repository’s [spacetime index theorem](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/22_theta_manifold_geometry/notes/01_physical_jet_geometry/04_SPACETIME_INDEX_AND_MARKED_TOPOLOGY_20261015.md) handles higher multiplicities as well. A spatial zero of multiplicity \(m\ge2\) contributes
\[
-\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor.
\]
Double and triple events contribute \(-1\); quadruple and quintuple events contribute \(-2\).

For a bounded Jordan region with analytic \(H\), no identically zero spatial slice, and a nonzero boundary jet, these contributions add:
\[
\boxed{
W(D):=\operatorname{wind}_{\partial D}(H+iH_x)
=
-\sum_{\text{collisions in }D}
\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor.
}
\]

**Therefore \(W(D)=0\) excludes every interior collision, including higher multiplicities.** For a general planar vector field, zero winding would allow positive and negative contributions to cancel. The heat equation supplies the additional sign restriction. This connection between parabolic zero counts and mapping degree is classical; [Angenent discusses it explicitly in §3](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~angenent/preprints/extatic.pdf).

This is where boundary winding changes the small-disk problem from our earlier conversation.

The direct approach tries to prove that the true jet stays away from zero throughout a region. In the approximation notation, it seeks a separation such as
\[
\|J_{f_N}\|>\varepsilon
\]
at every point that must be covered.

The boundary approach permits an unresolved interior. We might have a patch where our enclosures contain the origin, our retained sum nearly cancels, and no useful positive interior margin has been established. If we can surround that patch with a boundary whose true jet has winding zero, the index theorem excludes a collision anywhere inside.

That is a real difference in the information required. It does not guarantee that obtaining the boundary information will be easier.

In particular, **a boundary jet staying away from zero is necessary but insufficient**. The quadratic example has a perfectly nonzero boundary jet around its collision—and winding \(-1\). We must establish both boundary nonvanishing and the correct global winding.

One rigorous way to do that is to construct a boundary approximation \(\widetilde J\) satisfying
\[
\|J-\widetilde J\|<\|\widetilde J\|
\quad\text{everywhere on }\partial D.
\]
The straight-line deformation between the approximation and the true jet then cannot cross the origin. They have the same winding.

This allows a comparatively simple curve to represent the true boundary image. For example, complete enclosures might show that successive boundary segments lie in specified half-planes. A compatible polygon can then have its winding determined exactly. Every segment must be covered, including corners and cutoff transitions; sampled values and a visually smooth plot do not establish this.

A second useful feature is **integer-valued slack**. Once the hypotheses hold, \(W(D)\) is a nonpositive integer. Hence proving merely
\[
W(D)>-1
\]
already forces \(W(D)=0\).

In terms of total phase change,
\[
W(D)=\frac1{2\pi}
\oint_{\partial D}
\frac{H\,dH_x-H_x\,dH}{H^2+H_x^2}.
\]
We only need a rigorous lower bound on this integral greater than \(-2\pi\). We need not calculate its value to many decimal places.

That suggests an arithmetic question with a concrete tolerance:

> Can the complete arithmetic boundary contributions be bounded together tightly enough to rule out one full clockwise turn?

The word *together* matters. Different sides may contribute large phase changes that cancel. Bounding each side separately by absolute magnitude can discard precisely the information needed to get below a one-turn uncertainty. Also, directly estimating the displayed integral can become expensive because of its denominator and derivatives; a boundary homotopy or polygon certificate can sometimes avoid that calculation.

There is another interpretation through real-root counts. For a rectangle
\[
D=[t_-,t_+]\times[a,b],
\]
suppose \(H\) never vanishes on the spatial walls and all zeros on the two time faces are simple. If \(N_-\) and \(N_+\) are their real-root counts, then
\[
W(D)=\frac{N_--N_+}{2}.
\]
A double event produces two additional real roots as time increases, giving winding \(-1\). Equal counts imply no interior collision under these hypotheses.

This interpretation makes clear why the walls matter. If roots enter or leave through them, their contributions must be included. It also shows that simply assuming root counts remain unchanged would assume the very conclusion we want to prove.

For this investigation, I would begin with three connected questions:

1. **Where could the boundary be easier than the interior?** An unresolved small-jet patch is a natural candidate, provided we can enclose it completely and establish reliable boundary margins. The region need not be rectangular.

2. **What arithmetic information controls the boundary’s net turning?** Possibilities include a comparison with a reference jet of known winding, coherent bounds for paired boundary faces, or complete segment enclosures that preserve signs and correlations. Each needs an actual estimate using the genuine theta data.

3. **What would count as a gain?** A newly excluded region, a useful analytic boundary estimate, or a demonstrated reduction in the cost of obtaining a specified certificate.

The existing evidence is important here. The [GEO-T1 comparison](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/11_arithmetic_collision_rigidity/symmetries/notes/06_GEO_T1_WINDING_AND_DIRECT_COMPARISON_20261019.md) certified winding zero on
\[
[0.01,0.2]\times[999,1001].
\]
It used ten complete enclosure calls; optimized direct certification used seven. Shared source acquisition dominated both costs, and the box was already covered. That closes that particular comparison. It leaves open different domains, cheaper boundary acquisition, and new signed arithmetic estimates.

Likewise, topology alone cannot supply the missing arithmetic conclusion. The polynomial model above already defeats any generic claim that the heat equation forces zero winding. The repository’s [collision controls](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/12_collision_controls_and_screening.md) impose stronger screens: weighted-square controls lack full reflection, reflected smooth controls lack the theta square expansion, and Euler modifications alter the arithmetic coefficients. A proposed theta argument must use information that distinguishes it from the applicable control.

Finally, a finite zero-winding certificate excludes collisions only in its region. An RH application would require coverage of every possible positive-time event, including arbitrarily small positive times and sufficiently large heights. The positive-time confinement estimates in [Polymath’s Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S1.Thm5) help describe that coverage problem, but do not make it uniform down to time zero. The [result summary](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/13_local_heat_flow_geometry_and_rh_equivalent_criteria.md) and [criterion warning](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/avoid/01_restating_the_target.md) distinguish this global reformulation from a new estimate.

My preferred opening target is therefore quite specific: **find a completely enclosed region where direct estimates leave the interior unresolved, and identify arithmetic boundary information capable of proving zero winding.** That would test the distinctive advantage of this direction while keeping the missing theorem explicit.
It is probably best to focus on the situation where you are on the exact point where T=\Lambda (the De Bruijn Newman constant). Is that already something you are assuming here?
I’ll check how the boundary criterion specializes to \(T=\Lambda\), particularly what the threshold assumption adds and whether it changes the region we need to enclose.

**It was the motivating RH scenario, but it was not an assumption used in the boundary-winding argument I described.** That argument applies to any real collision. I agree that we should now focus specifically on a hypothetical collision at \(T=\Lambda>0\), because that gives us additional information.

The contradiction setup would be:
\[
\text{Assume RH fails. Then }T=\Lambda>0,
\]
and the repository’s [finite-collision reduction](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/quasi-rh/quasi-rh-exponent-descent/newman_collisions/newman_collision_reductions.tex) supplies a point \(x_*>0\) where
\[
H(T,x_*)=H_x(T,x_*)=0.
\]
We do not assume that the multiplicity is exactly two.

**Being at the threshold adds global information about the entire zero set:**

- At \(t=T\), **all zeros are real**, although some may be multiple.
- For \(t>T\), all zeros are real and simple.
- For \(t<T\), some nonreal zeros remain.

Thus, as time increases, \(T\) is the final transition to an entirely real zero set. Several collisions could occur simultaneously there. The threshold characterization and local splitting behavior are described in [Polymath’s paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S3).

An arbitrary earlier collision does not provide that global real-zero information. At the threshold, it gives additional constraints on logarithmic derivatives and higher derivatives—the source of the threshold inequalities discussed in the earlier chat. Those constraints might help control the boundary phase.

There is one important geometric distinction: **we focus on the event at \(T=\Lambda\), but the winding calculation still needs a neighborhood around it.** We would choose a small region containing \((T,x_*)\), with times on both sides:
\[
T-\delta<t<T+\delta,
\qquad 0<\delta<T.
\]
The boundary must avoid collisions. Putting the event itself on the boundary—for example, making \(t=T\) the upper face through \(x_*\)—would make the jet zero there, so ordinary boundary winding would be undefined.

For a sufficiently small region isolating an event of multiplicity \(m\), the existing theorem gives
\[
W(D)=-\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor\le-1.
\]
The research target becomes:

> Can the genuine theta arithmetic, **together with the all-real zero structure at the threshold**, force the boundary winding of a suitable enclosing region to be zero?

The threshold assumption does not itself force zero winding. Even the elementary model
\[
H(t,x)=x^2-2(t-T)
\]
has threshold \(T\), all-real zeros at and above it, and winding \(-1\) around its collision. The missing ingredient must still distinguish the genuine theta field.

Your proposed focus also sharpens the scope. **For an RH contradiction, it is enough to exclude a positive threshold event; we need not separately exclude every possible earlier, nonthreshold collision.** We would still need an argument covering every possible positive \(\Lambda\), event height, and multiplicity, since none is known in advance.

I’ll take **a hypothetical positive threshold \(T=\Lambda\), with its full real-zero constraints**, as our working setting from here. The next issue is precisely which of those extra constraints can yield useful information about the enclosing boundary.

100%, I think this sounds like a very strong program. I think excluding multiplicity 2 at first makes sense (if that is possible, it could be possible to do a recursive argument for higher multiplicities). Another route is to assume a positive \Lambda, and then show that there must be a larger \Lambda, that would also be a contradiction.

I’ll work through both ideas: starting with a double threshold zero, and using a hypothetical positive threshold to force nonreal zeros at a later time. I’ll also check what a passage to higher multiplicities would need.

Your “larger \(\Lambda\)” idea has a precise form: a collision at the supposed final threshold would force a later collision or nonreal zero of the same theta flow. Any strictly later witness would suffice; we would not need a uniform time gap. Local heat-flow splitting sends the colliding roots onto the real axis, so the later witness would have to come from additional arithmetic information. I’m using the write-page skill to record this and the multiplicity question in an incremental note.

There is a useful distinction between the two winding targets. Around the assumed threshold event, the collision forces winding \(-1\), and we would seek arithmetic information forcing \(0\). In a region entirely after the threshold, the threshold property forces winding \(0\), and your new route would seek arithmetic information forcing negative winding.

Higher multiplicity needs a separate reduction: differentiating can turn an \(m\)-fold zero into a double zero, but it changes the arithmetic function. A proof for the original theta field would need to remain valid after that change.

**Let’s make an ordinary double zero at a hypothetical positive threshold the first target.** Your second idea also gives a precise alternative contradiction: show that the supposed final threshold must be followed by another obstruction to real-rootedness.

The initial assumptions would be
\[
T=\Lambda>0,\qquad
H(T,x_*)=H_x(T,x_*)=0,\qquad
H_{xx}(T,x_*)\ne0.
\]
This fixes the simplest collision geometry while retaining the global information that all zeros of \(H_T\) are real.

The “larger \(\Lambda\)” idea should concern **the same unchanged theta flow**. Its threshold is unique. If the assumed event forced a nonreal zero at some later time \(t_1>T\), the threshold characterization would give
\[
\Lambda>t_1>T=\Lambda,
\]
an immediate contradiction. Increasing an upper bound on \(\Lambda\), or finding a larger threshold for a modified function, would not have that consequence.

A later real multiple zero would also suffice: its local splitting produces nonreal zeros immediately before that later event, at times we could choose still greater than \(T\). These implications follow from the threshold characterization and [Polymath’s local splitting theorem](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S3).

**Any strictly later witness is enough.** The time separation may depend on the hypothetical event and be arbitrarily small. We would not need a uniform increment or an infinite iteration.

This gives two distinct boundary-winding targets:

| Region | What the hypothetical threshold forces | What arithmetic would need to force |
|---|---|---|
| A small region enclosing the double event at \(T\) | Winding \(-1\) | Winding \(0\) |
| A region lying entirely after \(T\) | Winding \(0\) | Negative winding |

In the second row, all zeros after \(T\) are real and simple, so there are no physical jet zeros. Negative winding would force a later collision and contradict that fact.

Your proposal therefore reverses the arithmetic objective: **instead of proving that the assumed event cannot occur locally, prove that it cannot be the final event.** That is a useful alternative formulation, although we still need the arithmetic mechanism that would force the later witness.

One existing calculation helps locate that difficulty. Define
\[
\mathcal L(t,x)=H_x^2-HH_{xx}.
\]
For the theta field at an all-real time, \(\mathcal L\ge0\) on the real axis. Thus proving \(\mathcal L(t_1,x_1)<0\) somewhere after \(T\) would supply a contradiction.

But at the assumed double event, the heat equation gives
\[
\mathcal L(T+s,x_*)
=s\,H_{xx}(T,x_*)^2+O(s^2)>0
\]
for sufficiently small \(s>0\). The immediate local evolution has the permitted sign. A later negative witness would require additional arithmetic information beyond that local expansion.

On higher multiplicities, starting with \(m=2\) is sensible, but **a recursive extension needs its own justification**. Differentiating \(m-2\) times turns an \(m\)-fold zero into a double zero and preserves the heat equation; it changes the arithmetic function, however. A theorem proved specifically for \(H\) cannot automatically be applied to its derivatives.

There is a potentially cleaner possibility: the topological theorem already covers every multiplicity through
\[
\operatorname{ind}J=-\lfloor m/2\rfloor.
\]
If the successful arithmetic boundary estimate can be formulated without requiring \(H_{xx}\ne0\), it might extend directly. Otherwise, we would need a reduction preserving its arithmetic hypotheses. Excluding double events alone would leave higher-multiplicity threshold events unresolved.
